module_title: Uniform Civil Code & Special Marriage Act: Foundational Concepts
introduction: This foundational level explores the constitutional mandate for a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) and introduces the Special Marriage Act (SMA), 1954—India's existing secular framework that acts as a 'mini-UCC' for couples who wish to marry outside their personal religious laws.

core_concepts.title: Article 44: The Uniform Civil Code (UCC)
core_concepts.description:
Article 44 is a Directive Principle of State Policy (DPSP) under Part IV of the Constitution.
- The Mandate: 'The State shall endeavor to secure for the citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.'
- Meaning: A UCC aims to replace personal laws based on the scriptures and customs of each major religious community with a common set of laws governing every citizen in matters of marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption.
- Justiciability: Like all DPSPs, Article 44 is non-justiciable (cannot be enforced by a court), but it acts as a guiding principle for governance.

core_concepts.title: Special Marriage Act (SMA), 1954
core_concepts.description:
The SMA is a secular, civil law governing marriages in India. 
- Purpose: It allows any two individuals (irrespective of their religion, caste, or nationality) to marry each other without either party having to convert to the other's religion.
- Scope: Unlike the Hindu Marriage Act or Muslim Personal Law, the SMA applies to ALL citizens of India and to Indian nationals living abroad.

core_concepts.title: Conditions for Marriage under SMA (Section 4)
core_concepts.description:
The conditions mirror the secular standards of capacity:
1. Monogamy: Neither party has a spouse living.
2. Mental Capacity: Neither party is incapable of giving valid consent due to unsoundness of mind.
3. Age: The male has completed 21 years and the female has completed 18 years.
4. Prohibited Degrees: The parties are not within the degrees of prohibited relationship (unless a recognized custom of at least one party permits it).

core_concepts.title: The Procedure: The 30-Day Notice (Sections 5 to 7)
core_concepts.description:
A marriage under SMA is not instantaneous. 
- Section 5: The parties must give written notice to the Marriage Officer of the district where at least one party has resided for at least 30 days.
- Section 6 & 7: The notice is published/displayed. Anyone can object to the marriage within **30 days** on the ground that it violates Section 4 conditions (e.g., one party is already married or underage).

important_entities.name: The Constitutional Friction (Art 25 vs Art 44)
important_entities.key_fact: The core debate surrounding the implementation of the UCC.
important_entities.significance: Opponents of the UCC argue that it violates Article 25 (Freedom of Religion), which protects the right to practice religious customs (including personal laws). Proponents argue that secularism and Article 14 (Equality) demand a UCC, especially to eradicate gender discriminatory practices embedded in traditional personal laws.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will propose a scenario: 'A Hindu male and a Muslim female wish to marry. Under the SMA, the female must convert to Hinduism before the marriage is registered.' This is completely **FALSE**. The entire purpose of the Special Marriage Act is to facilitate inter-faith marriages *without* requiring religious conversion.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Age limits are 21/18. You must live in the district for 30 days before giving notice. You must wait 30 days after the notice before marrying.

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a question asks 'Which legislation provides a secular framework for inter-faith marriages in India?', the answer is the **Special Marriage Act, 1954**.
